title: Slow it down

segments.voice: Yesterday, prana: breath, and the life that moves with it. Your line was it breathes you. Today, for the first time, you change it. Gently.

A hard email, a slammed door, a long line at the pharmacy. Heart pounding, jaw tight, and somebody says: just breathe. It's annoying advice, mostly because nobody ever says how. Faster? Deeper? Hold it until the feeling passes? Here's the how, and it's very simple. You don't need to breathe in more. You need to breathe out longer. Today's practice is two numbers: four, and six.
screen: `JUST BREATHE. BUT HOW?` → `NOT MORE IN.` → `LONGER OUT.`

segments.voice: Today, a first, gentle change. Breathe in through the nose for a count of four. Then breathe out, through the nose if you can, for a count of six. No holding, no forcing. Just an out-breath a little longer than the in-breath. Why does it work? Many yoga teachers today describe the out-breath as the settling, releasing half. And you can notice something in your own body: your heart speeds up a little as you breathe in, and slows a little as you breathe out. Try it with a hand on your chest sometime. So when the out-breath is longer, you spend more of each minute in the slowing part. That's not a promise of anything; it's just something you can feel. The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali, a classic text of yoga, describe breath practice as regulating the flow of the in-breath and the out-breath, and say it can become long and subtle. That's the direction. To keep it safe: if six feels like a strain, use three in and five out. If you get dizzy, stop and breathe normally. The count isn't a test. What matters is the shape: slow it down, and let the out-breath be the long one. Longer out.
screen: `FOUR IN, SIX OUT.` · `THE HEART SLOWS ON THE OUT-BREATH.` · `LONG AND SUBTLE.` · `IF IT STRAINS, SHORTEN IT.` · then, large: `LONGER OUT.`

segments.voice: Sit tall and soft, take one ordinary breath to arrive, then breathe in through the nose for four and out slowly for six, counting quietly in your head at whatever speed feels natural. Don't hold at the top or the bottom; just slow, even, and a longer out. If it strains, shorten both numbers.
Out-breath, the half of the breath you lengthen: four counts in, six counts out, the first change this practice makes to the breath.
Your line: longer out. Four in, six out, whenever you need it. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many yoga teachers in the Hindu tradition begin breath practice with slow, even breathing through the nose, making the exhale longer than the inhale, before moving to more advanced pranayama.

fork.setup: you're doing four in, six out, and by the third round you feel a bit dizzy. what do you do?
fork.reveal: stop, and breathe normally. then try a shorter count, like three in and five out. the count isn't a test.

trapdoor: what you thought: just breathe means breathe deep.
what it means: slow it down, and make the out-breath the long one: four in, six out.
what a scholar hears: Yoga Sutras 2.50 describe regulated breath as long and subtle; the heart's rise and fall with the breath is called respiratory sinus arrhythmia.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutras of Patanjali 2.49–2.50 (pranayama; breath made long and subtle)

notes: Yoga Sutras 2.50: pranayama described as external, internal and suspended, regulated by place, time and number, becoming long (dirgha) and subtle (sukshma). Paraphrased. Confirm.
Heart rate rising on inhale and falling on exhale (respiratory sinus arrhythmia) is well established; stated as something you can feel, with no health claim. Confirm.
Safety: shorter count if strained; stop if dizzy. Consider adding a general note in-app for people with respiratory or heart conditions.
